title: Differentiate between supervised, unsupervised, and reinforcement learning paradigms based on input data and learning targets.
answer_html: Supervised learning uses labeled input and target data. Unsupervised learning discovers hidden patterns in unlabeled data. Reinforcement learning learns optimal actions to maximize rewards in an environment.

title: List any four key stages of the 7-Step Machine Learning Lifecycle.
answer_html: Four key stages are: Data Collection, Data Preprocessing, Model Training, and Model Evaluation/Deployment.

title: What is Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA), and what is its primary objective during data preprocessing?
answer_html: EDA involves analyzing datasets to summarize their main characteristics, often using statistical graphics. Its objective is to discover patterns, spot anomalies, and check assumptions before formal modeling.

title: Explain the significance of feature engineering in preparing raw datasets for model training.
answer_html: Feature engineering transforms raw data into meaningful features that better represent the underlying problem to predictive models, thereby improving model accuracy on unseen data.

title: Why is categorical label encoding required before passing categorical features into a machine learning algorithm?
answer_html: Most machine learning algorithms require numerical inputs to perform mathematical computations. Categorical label encoding converts string/categorical variables into numerical values so models can process them.

title: Mention two common strategies for handling missing values during data cleaning.
answer_html: Two common strategies are: 1) Removing rows/columns with missing data, and 2) Imputing missing values using the mean, median, or mode.

title: What is the role of data normalization and feature scaling in model fitting?
answer_html: Normalization and feature scaling ensure that features with different scales contribute equally to model fitting and prevent features with larger ranges from dominating the objective function.

title: Define model fitting and state why model validation is necessary.
answer_html: Model fitting is the process of adjusting a model's parameters to best align with training data. Model validation is necessary to ensure the model generalizes well to unseen data and isn't overfitted.

title: Distinguish between data collection/fetching strategies and feature selection.
answer_html: Data collection involves gathering raw data from various sources, while feature selection involves choosing the most relevant subset of features from the collected data to build a model.

title: What is the historical significance of model training in the evolution of Machine Learning?
answer_html: Model training shifted the paradigm from explicitly programming rules to allowing algorithms to automatically infer patterns and rules from historical data.

title: Name two common visualization techniques used during EDA to inspect data distributions.
answer_html: Two common techniques are Histograms (to view distributions of single variables) and Scatter Plots (to view relationships between two variables).

title: Explain the difference between independent variables (predictors) and dependent variables (targets).
answer_html: Independent variables (predictors) are the inputs used to make predictions. The dependent variable (target) is the output or outcome being predicted by the model.

title: Why is Python widely chosen as a foundational language for machine learning data pipelines?
answer_html: Python has a rich ecosystem of specialized libraries (like Scikit-Learn, Pandas, NumPy), an intuitive syntax, and extensive community support, making it highly efficient for building ML pipelines.

title: What constitutes a fundamental model validation workflow in the 7-step ML lifecycle?
answer_html: It typically involves splitting data into training and testing sets, training the model on the train set, and evaluating its performance on the unseen test set using specific metrics.

title: Write the hypothesis function for a Simple Linear Regression model and define its components.
answer_html: The hypothesis function is h(x) = θ0 + θ1*x, where θ0 is the y-intercept, θ1 is the slope (weight), and x is the input feature.

title: State the equation for Multiple Linear Regression with n independent variables.
answer_html: The equation is y = θ0 + θ1*x1 + θ2*x2 + ... + θn*xn, where θi are the coefficients and xi are the independent variables.

title: Define residual error ei in linear regression analysis.
answer_html: Residual error ei is the difference between the actual observed value yi and the predicted value ŷi from the linear regression model: ei = yi - ŷi.

title: State the primary mathematical objective of the Ordinary Least Squares (OLS) method.
answer_html: The primary objective of OLS is to find the line of best fit by minimizing the sum of the squared residual errors between the observed and predicted values.

title: Write the Mean Squared Error (MSE) cost function Jθ used in linear regression.
answer_html: The MSE cost function is J(θ) = (1/2m) Σ (hθ(xi) - yi)², where m is the number of training examples.

title: Why is Gradient Descent preferred over the analytical Normal Equation for high-dimensional datasets?
answer_html: Gradient Descent is computationally much faster for high-dimensional datasets with many features, whereas the Normal Equation requires inverting an n x n matrix, which scales poorly as O(n³).

title: What is the learning rate α in Gradient Descent, and what happens if it is set too high?
answer_html: The learning rate α determines the step size taken in the direction of the gradient. If it is set too high, Gradient Descent may overshoot the minimum and fail to converge or diverge entirely.

title: Define Polynomial Regression and explain how it captures non-linear data trends.
answer_html: Polynomial Regression models the relationship between independent and dependent variables as an nth-degree polynomial, allowing the model curve to bend and capture non-linear trends in the data.

title: Is Polynomial Regression considered a linear or non-linear model? Explain briefly.
answer_html: It is considered a linear model because, although the features are raised to a power (non-linear data transformations), the model is still linear with respect to its parameters (the coefficients).

title: Define Overfitting and list two common causes.
answer_html: Overfitting occurs when a model learns the training data too well, including its noise, leading to poor generalization. Common causes include overly complex models and training on insufficient/noisy data.

title: Define Underfitting and mention how it can be identified.
answer_html: Underfitting occurs when a model is too simple to capture the underlying pattern of the data. It can be identified when the model shows poor performance (high error) on both the training and validation sets.

title: Explain the Bias-Variance tradeoff in the context of model complexity.
answer_html: The Tradeoff implies that as model complexity increases, bias decreases but variance increases (causing overfitting). Lower complexity increases bias but decreases variance (causing underfitting). The goal is a balance minimizing total error.

title: State two techniques to reduce overfitting in regression models.
answer_html: Two techniques are adding Regularization (L1/L2) to the cost function and reducing model complexity (e.g., feature selection or pruning).

title: What is Regularization, and why is it added to regression cost functions?
answer_html: Regularization involves adding a penalty term to the cost function to constrain or shrink the model weights. It is added to prevent overfitting and improve generalization on new data.

title: Differentiate between Ridge L2 and Lasso L1 regularization penalties.
answer_html: Ridge (L2) adds a penalty equal to the sum of the squared magnitude of coefficients. Lasso (L1) adds a penalty equal to the sum of the absolute values of the coefficients.

title: Why does Lasso L1 regularization perform automatic feature selection while Ridge L2 does not?
answer_html: Lasso (L1) tends to shrink less important feature coefficients exactly to zero, effectively performing feature selection. Ridge (L2) shrinks them near zero but rarely exactly to zero.

title: Write the mathematical formula for Mean Absolute Error (MAE).
answer_html: The formula is MAE = (1/n) Σ |yi - ŷi|, where yi is actual, ŷi is predicted, and n is the number of samples.

title: State the formula for Root Mean Squared Error (RMSE) and explain its advantage over MSE.
answer_html: RMSE = √((1/n) Σ (yi - ŷi)²). Its advantage is that it penalizes larger errors more heavily than MAE and shares the same units as the target variable.

title: What does the R2 (R-squared) coefficient measure, and what is its standard range?
answer_html: R-squared measures the proportion of variance in the dependent variable explained by the independent variables. Its standard range is between 0 and 1.

title: Why is Adjusted R2 preferred over standard R2 in Multiple Linear Regression?
answer_html: Standard R2 artificially increases when any new variable is added. Adjusted R2 penalizes the addition of non-significant predictors, giving a more accurate measure of fit for multiple predictors.

title: Write the Sigmoid activation function formula and state its output range.
answer_html: The Sigmoid formula is σ(z) = 1 / (1 + e^(-z)). Its output range is continuously between 0 and 1, making it ideal for probability estimation.

title: What is the standard threshold value used in Logistic Regression for binary classification?
answer_html: The standard threshold value is 0.5. If the predicted probability is ≥ 0.5, the class is predicted as 1; if < 0.5, the class is predicted as 0.

title: Write the single-sample log-loss (binary cross-entropy) cost function formula.
answer_html: The formula is Cost = - [y * log(ŷ) + (1 - y) * log(1 - ŷ)], where y is the true label (0 or 1) and ŷ is the predicted probability.

title: Define a decision boundary in a binary classification problem.
answer_html: A decision boundary is a hyperplane or surface that separates the feature space into two distinct regions, classifying data points into one of the two binary classes.

title: Explain the core working mechanism of the K-Nearest Neighbors (KNN) algorithm.
answer_html: KNN classifies a new data point based on the majority class among its 'K' closest neighbors in the feature space, calculated using a distance metric like Euclidean distance.

title: State the formula for Euclidean distance between two points in n-dimensional space.
answer_html: The formula is d(p, q) = √(Σ (qi - pi)²) from i=1 to n, where p and q are two points with n features.

title: What happens to KNN classification performance if K is set too small or too large?
answer_html: If K is too small, the model becomes highly sensitive to noise (overfitting). If K is too large, the decision boundary becomes overly smooth, potentially missing local patterns (underfitting).

title: Define Entropy in Information Theory and write its mathematical equation.
answer_html: Entropy measures the uncertainty or impurity in a dataset. Its equation is H(S) = - Σ p_i * log2(p_i), where p_i is the proportion of elements in class i.

title: Define Information Gain and explain its role in building Decision Trees.
answer_html: Information Gain is the reduction in Entropy achieved by splitting a dataset on a specific attribute. Decision Trees use it to select the best feature to split on at each node (the one with the highest gain).

title: State the Gini Impurity formula used for evaluating node splits in Decision Trees.
answer_html: The Gini Impurity formula is Gini = 1 - Σ (p_i)², where p_i is the probability of an item belonging to class i. It measures how often a randomly chosen element would be incorrectly labeled.

title: State Bayes' Theorem formula and label each term ((P(A|B), P(B| A), P(A), P(B)).
answer_html: P(A|B) = [P(B|A) * P(A)] / P(B). P(A|B) is posterior probability, P(B|A) is likelihood, P(A) is prior probability, and P(B) is the marginal probability of evidence.

title: Why is the Naive Bayes classifier termed "naive"?
answer_html: It is called "naive" because it makes the strong, often unrealistic assumption that all features are conditionally independent of each other given the class label.

title: Define a Hyperplane and Support Vectors in Support Vector Machines (SVM).
answer_html: A Hyperplane is the linear decision boundary that separates classes. Support Vectors are the data points located closest to the hyperplane, which directly influence its position and orientation.

title: Differentiate between Hard Margin SVM and Soft Margin SVM.
answer_html: Hard Margin SVM strictly separates classes without allowing any misclassifications (sensitive to outliers). Soft Margin SVM introduces a slack variable to allow some misclassifications, improving generalization on noisy data.

title: Explain the purpose of Kernel functions (e.g., RBF, Polynomial) in SVM.
answer_html: Kernel functions compute the dot product of data points in a transformed, higher-dimensional feature space, enabling SVM to find linear decision boundaries for complex, non-linearly separable data.

title: Describe the voting structure and ensemble approach used in Random Forests.
answer_html: Random Forests build multiple decision trees independently using bootstrapped data and random feature subsets. For classification, the final output is decided by a majority vote among all the individual trees.

title: Name three popular boosting ensemble algorithms covered in statistical classification.
answer_html: Three popular boosting algorithms are AdaBoost (Adaptive Boosting), Gradient Boosting Machine (GBM), and XGBoost (Extreme Gradient Boosting).

title: Write the mathematical formulas for Precision, Recall, and F1-Score.
answer_html: Precision = TP / (TP + FP), Recall = TP / (TP + FN), F1-Score = 2 * (Precision * Recall) / (Precision + Recall), where TP=True Positives, FP=False Positives, FN=False Negatives.

title: Explain the three main machine learning paradigms (Supervised, Unsupervised, and Reinforcement Learning) with their key characteristics and input data requirements.
answer_html: Supervised Learning: Uses labeled training data to predict outcomes. Unsupervised Learning: Uses unlabeled data to find hidden patterns (e.g., clustering). Reinforcement Learning: Learns by interacting with an environment to maximize cumulative rewards.

title: Describe the first three sequential stages of the 7-Step Machine Learning Lifecycle in data pipeline design.
answer_html: The first three stages are: 1) Data Collection: Gathering raw data from various sources. 2) Data Preparation/Cleaning: Handling missing values, outliers, and duplicates. 3) Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA): Analyzing data distributions and relationships using statistics and visualization.

title: Detail the importance of data cleaning principles and outline two strategies for handling missing values.
answer_html: Data cleaning ensures high data quality, preventing poor model performance. Two strategies for missing values: 1) Imputation: Filling missing cells with the mean, median, or mode. 2) Deletion: Removing rows or columns that have excessive missing values.

title: Define Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA) and explain how data visualization techniques aid in discovering dataset distributions.
answer_html: EDA is the process of visually and statistically summarizing the main characteristics of a dataset. Visualization techniques like histograms and box plots help reveal data distributions, skewness, and outliers intuitively.

title: Explain the role of Feature Engineering and distinguish it from feature selection.
answer_html: Feature Engineering: Creating new features or transforming existing ones to improve model performance. Feature Selection: Choosing a subset of the most relevant original features, discarding redundant or irrelevant ones to simplify the model.

title: Why is categorical label encoding necessary in machine learning data preprocessing prior to model fitting?
answer_html: Machine learning algorithms perform mathematical computations and require numerical input. Categorical label encoding (like One-Hot Encoding or Label Encoding) transforms string/text labels into numerical representations so algorithms can process them.

title: Differentiate between feature normalization and feature scaling, stating why they are applied before model fitting.
answer_html: Feature Scaling: Adjusting feature values to a standard range (e.g., Min-Max scaling to [0,1]). Feature Normalization: Adjusting the distribution to have a mean of 0 and standard deviation of 1 (Z-score normalization). Both ensure no single feature dominates the objective function due to scale.

title: Explain the concept and significance of model training within the overall machine learning lifecycle.
answer_html: Model training is the core phase where an algorithm learns patterns from the provided dataset by optimizing its parameters (e.g., weights in regression) to minimize the error or loss function, establishing the mapping from inputs to outputs.

title: Describe fundamental validation strategies used to evaluate the performance of a trained machine learning model.
answer_html: Validation strategies include: 1) Train-Test Split: Partitioning data into a training set and a testing set. 2) K-Fold Cross Validation: Dividing data into K folds, training on K-1 folds and testing on the remaining fold iteratively to ensure robust evaluation.

title: Differentiate between independent predictor variables and dependent target variables using a concrete example.
answer_html: Independent Predictor Variables: The inputs or features used to make predictions (e.g., house size, location). Dependent Target Variables: The output or outcome being predicted by the model (e.g., house price).

title: Explain how raw data collection and fetching strategies impact the downstream efficiency of an ML pipeline.
answer_html: Efficient data collection directly affects the quality and quantity of data available. High-quality, representative data fetched seamlessly reduces preprocessing overhead and improves the final model's predictive accuracy and reliability.

title: Outline the historical evolution and structural taxonomy of machine learning paradigms.
answer_html: Machine learning evolved from early logical rules to statistical learning, and now deep neural networks. Its structural taxonomy primarily divides into Supervised, Unsupervised, Semi-supervised, and Reinforcement Learning, based on the availability of labeled feedback.

title: Explain how computing statistical summaries on raw data helps in initial data understanding during EDA.
answer_html: Statistical summaries (mean, median, standard deviation, quartiles) provide a quick numerical overview of the dataset's central tendency and dispersion, highlighting potential anomalies, outliers, and scaling requirements before visual analysis.

title: Why can raw unstructured/uncleaned datasets not be directly fed into standard machine learning algorithms?
answer_html: Standard ML algorithms require numerical, well-structured, tabular data without missing values or infinite entries. Raw data often contains text, noise, inconsistencies, and missing fields, causing algorithms to fail or produce garbage outputs.

title: Write the structural mathematical formulation for a Simple Linear Regression model and explain all its terms.
answer_html: Formula: y = β0 + β1x + ε. y: Dependent target variable. x: Independent predictor variable. β0: Y-intercept (value of y when x=0). β1: Slope coefficient (change in y for a 1-unit change in x). ε: Error term.

title: Explain Multiple Linear Regression and state its algebraic equation for n independent variables.
answer_html: Multiple Linear Regression extends simple regression to model the relationship between one continuous dependent variable and multiple independent variables. Equation: y = β0 + β1x1 + β2x2 + ... + βnxn + ε.

title: Define residual error in linear regression and explain its geometric interpretation.
answer_html: A residual error is the difference between the actual observed value and the predicted value (e = y - ŷ). Geometrically, it represents the vertical distance from a data point to the fitted regression line.

title: Explain the Ordinary Least Squares (OLS) estimation method and state the objective function it minimizes.
answer_html: Ordinary Least Squares (OLS) is a method that estimates regression coefficients by minimizing the sum of the squared residuals. Objective function: Minimize Σ(yi - ŷi)².

title: Describe the role of the Mean Squared Error (MSE) cost function J(θ) in optimizing regression parameters.
answer_html: MSE averages the squared differences between predicted and actual values. In optimizing regression parameters, the MSE serves as the cost function J(θ); the algorithm (like Gradient Descent) minimizes J(θ) to find the best-fitting weights.

title: Explain how Gradient Descent updates parameters iteratively to find the optimal slope and intercept.
answer_html: Gradient Descent calculates the partial derivatives (gradient) of the cost function with respect to the slope and intercept. It then updates these parameters iteratively in the opposite direction of the gradient by a step size (learning rate) to reach the minimum cost.

title: Define the learning rate (α) in Gradient Descent and explain the consequences of setting it too high or too low.
answer_html: The learning rate (α) determines the step size at each iteration. If α is too high, the algorithm may overshoot the minimum and diverge. If α is too low, convergence will be exceedingly slow and might get stuck in local minima.

title: Explain Polynomial Regression and state how higher-degree terms allow it to capture non-linear data trends.
answer_html: Polynomial regression models the relationship as an nth degree polynomial (e.g., y = β0 + β1x + β2x²). The higher-degree terms introduce curves, allowing the model to fit non-linear patterns in the data.

title: Discuss why Polynomial Regression is technically classified as a linear model despite fitting non-linear curves.
answer_html: It is technically a linear model because the regression equation is linear in its parameters (the coefficients β). The relationship between the parameters and the dependent variable remains linear, even though the features (x², x³) are non-linear.

title: Explain Overfitting in regression models and state two practical techniques to detect and prevent it.
answer_html: Overfitting occurs when a model learns the training data and its noise too well, performing poorly on unseen data. Detection: High training accuracy, low validation accuracy. Prevention: 1) Cross-validation. 2) Regularization (L1/L2).

title: Explain Underfitting, its primary root causes, and how its error profile differs from overfitting.
answer_html: Underfitting happens when a model is too simple to capture the underlying patterns in the data (high bias). Root causes: Insufficient model complexity or inadequate features. Error profile: High training error and high validation error.

title: Describe the Bias-Variance tradeoff and how model complexity influences bias and variance.
answer_html: Bias is error from erroneous assumptions (underfitting); variance is error from sensitivity to small fluctuations in training data (overfitting). Increasing model complexity typically decreases bias but increases variance. The tradeoff seeks the optimal balance.

title: Explain the principle of Regularization and why penalty terms are added to the regression loss function.
answer_html: Regularization prevents overfitting by adding a penalty term to the loss function based on the magnitude of the model's coefficients. This discourages overly complex models with extremely large weights.

title: Compare Ridge L2 and Lasso L1 regression with respect to their mathematical penalty terms and impact on weights.
answer_html: Ridge (L2): Adds a penalty proportional to the sum of squared weights (λΣw²). It shrinks weights but rarely to zero. Lasso (L1): Adds a penalty proportional to the sum of absolute weights (λΣ|w|). It can force some weights exactly to zero.

title: Explain why Lasso L1 regularization performs automatic feature selection whereas Ridge L2 shrinks coefficients without zeroing them.
answer_html: Lasso's L1 penalty has a diamond-shaped constraint region, and the loss function's elliptical contours often intersect it at the corners where some coefficients are exactly zero, performing feature selection. Ridge's circular constraint region usually intersects without zeroing coefficients.

title: Write the mathematical formulas for Mean Absolute Error (MAE) and Mean Squared Error (MSE) and highlight their differences.
answer_html: MAE: (1/n) Σ|yi - ŷi|. MSE: (1/n) Σ(yi - ŷi)². Differences: MSE heavily penalizes large errors because of the squaring operation, whereas MAE treats all errors proportionally and is more robust to outliers.

title: Define Root Mean Squared Error (RMSE) and explain its interpretive advantage over Mean Squared Error (MSE).
answer_html: RMSE: √((1/n) Σ(yi - ŷi)²). The interpretive advantage of RMSE is that it expresses the error in the exact same units as the original dependent target variable, making it easier to understand practically than MSE.

title: Explain the R2 (R-squared) goodness-of-fit metric and distinguish it from Adjusted R2 in multiple regression.
answer_html: R-squared measures the proportion of variance in the dependent variable explained by the model (0 to 1). Adjusted R-squared modifies R² by penalizing the addition of unnecessary independent variables, preventing artificial score inflation in multiple regression.

title: Write the mathematical formula for the Sigmoid activation function and explain how it converts real values into probabilities.
answer_html: Formula: σ(z) = 1 / (1 + e^(-z)). The Sigmoid function takes any real-valued number (z) and maps it into a smooth S-curve bounded between 0 and 1, allowing the output to be interpreted as a probability.

title: Explain how binary decision boundaries are defined and applied in Logistic Regression using a probability threshold.
answer_html: Logistic regression outputs a probability between 0 and 1. A threshold (typically 0.5) is defined: if p ≥ 0.5, the class is predicted as 1; if p < 0.5, class 0. This threshold establishes a linear decision boundary separating the classes.

title: Write the single-sample log-loss (binary cross-entropy) formula and explain why MSE is unsuitable for classification.
answer_html: Formula: Loss = -[y*log(p) + (1-y)*log(1-p)]. MSE is unsuitable for classification because when used with a sigmoid activation, it creates a non-convex loss function with multiple local minima, preventing gradient descent from finding the global minimum.

title: Describe the complete step-by-step working mechanics of the K-Nearest Neighbors (KNN) classification algorithm.
answer_html: 1) Choose the number of neighbors, K. 2) Calculate the distance (e.g., Euclidean) between the new data point and all training points. 3) Sort the distances and select the K nearest neighbors. 4) Assign the new point to the majority class among those K neighbors.

title: Write the Euclidean distance formula between two points in n-dimensional space and explain its purpose in KNN.
answer_html: Formula: d = √(Σ(xi - yi)²) from i=1 to n. In KNN, it quantifies the geometric similarity or 'closeness' between the test instance and training instances to identify the nearest neighbors.

title: Discuss how selecting an optimal value of K affects KNN predictions and model generalization.
answer_html: A small K (e.g., K=1) makes the model highly sensitive to noise, leading to high variance (overfitting). A large K smooths decision boundaries but can oversimplify the model, leading to high bias (underfitting). The optimal K balances this tradeoff.

title: Define Entropy in Information Theory, write its mathematical expression, and state what zero entropy signifies.
answer_html: Entropy measures the level of impurity or uncertainty in a dataset. Formula: H(S) = -Σ(p_i * log2(p_i)). An entropy of zero signifies a perfectly pure dataset where all examples belong to exactly one single class.

title: Explain Information Gain and describe how a Decision Tree algorithm uses it to select optimal node splits.
answer_html: Information Gain is the expected reduction in entropy after splitting a dataset on a specific attribute. Decision Trees calculate Information Gain for all available features and choose the one with the highest gain to split the node, maximizing class purity.

title: Define Gini Impurity, state its mathematical formula, and compare its computational efficiency against Entropy.
answer_html: Gini Impurity measures the probability of incorrectly classifying a randomly chosen element. Formula: Gini = 1 - Σ(p_i)². It is computationally more efficient than Entropy because it does not require calculating logarithmic functions.

title: State Bayes' Theorem formula, define each term (Prior, Likelihood, Posterior, Evidence), and explain its role in classification.
answer_html: Formula: P(A|B) = [P(B|A) * P(A)] / P(B). Prior (P(A)): Initial probability of class. Likelihood (P(B|A)): Probability of predictor given class. Posterior (P(A|B)): Updated probability. Evidence (P(B)): Total probability of predictor. It's used to calculate the probability of a class given the features.

title: Explain the conditional feature independence assumption in the Naive Bayes classifier and why it is termed 'naive'.
answer_html: Naive Bayes assumes that the presence of one feature is completely unrelated and independent of the presence of any other feature, given the class label. It is termed 'naive' because this strict independence rarely holds completely true in real-world data.

title: Define Hyperplane, Support Vectors, and Margin in Support Vector Machines (SVM).
answer_html: Hyperplane: The decision boundary that separates classes. Support Vectors: The data points closest to the hyperplane that influence its position. Margin: The perpendicular distance between the hyperplane and the closest support vectors.

title: Differentiate between Hard Margin SVM and Soft Margin SVM, explaining how slack variables/hinge loss handle non-separable data.
answer_html: Hard Margin SVM strictly requires all data points to be correctly classified, working only for perfectly linearly separable data. Soft Margin SVM introduces slack variables (and hinge loss) to allow some misclassifications or margin violations, handling non-separable data gracefully.

title: Explain the Kernel trick in SVM and how it allows linear separation of non-linearly separable data in higher dimensions.
answer_html: The Kernel trick uses kernel functions (like RBF or Polynomial) to compute the dot product of data points in a higher-dimensional space without explicitly transforming them. This makes it possible to find a linear separating hyperplane for data that is non-linear in its original space.

title: Describe the ensemble structure, bagging mechanics, and voting system used in Random Forest models.
answer_html: Random Forest is an ensemble of many Decision Trees. It uses Bagging (Bootstrap Aggregating) to train each tree on a random subset of data with replacement. For prediction, it uses a voting system (majority vote for classification, average for regression) across all trees.

title: Differentiate between Bagging (e.g., Random Forest) and Boosting ensemble techniques (e.g., AdaBoost, XGBoost).
answer_html: Bagging builds multiple independent models in parallel to reduce variance (e.g., Random Forest). Boosting builds models sequentially, where each new model focuses on correcting the errors made by the previous ones, aiming to reduce bias (e.g., XGBoost).

title: Construct a 2 * 2 Confusion Matrix and write the formulas for Accuracy, Precision, Recall, and F1-Score.
answer_html: Matrix: [[TP, FN], [FP, TN]]. Accuracy: (TP+TN)/(TP+TN+FP+FN). Precision: TP/(TP+FP). Recall: TP/(TP+FN). F1-Score: 2 * (Precision * Recall) / (Precision + Recall).

title: Explain why F1-Score is a more reliable metric than Accuracy when evaluating models on imbalanced datasets.
answer_html: In imbalanced datasets, Accuracy can be misleadingly high if the model simply predicts the majority class every time. F1-Score balances Precision and Recall, ensuring the model performs well on the minority (often more important) class by taking both false positives and false negatives into account.

title: 1. Explain the 7-Step Machine Learning Lifecycle in detail, highlighting the core objectives of data cleaning, data preprocessing, and model validation.
answer_html:
7-Step Machine Learning Lifecycle

The machine learning lifecycle consists of seven sequential steps that convert raw data into a functional predictive model.

  • 1. Data Gathering: Identifying and collecting relevant datasets from various sources (databases, APIs, web scraping).
  • 2. Data Preparation/Cleaning: The objective is to fix missing values, remove duplicates, and handle outliers. It ensures the data is accurate and consistent.
  • 3. Data Preprocessing & EDA: Exploring the data to find patterns. Preprocessing involves feature scaling, normalization, and encoding categorical variables.
  • 4. Data Split: Dividing the dataset into training and testing sets (e.g., 80/20 split) to ensure unbiased evaluation.
  • 5. Model Training: Selecting an appropriate algorithm and feeding the training data into it to let the model learn the underlying patterns.
  • 6. Model Evaluation/Validation: The objective is to test the trained model on unseen testing data to measure its performance using metrics like accuracy, RMSE, or F1-Score.
  • 7. Prediction & Deployment: Deploying the validated model into a production environment to make predictions on real-world, live data.

title: 2. Compare Supervised, Unsupervised, and Reinforcement Learning paradigms with respect to input data requirements, feedback loops, and practical target applications.
answer_html:
Comparison of Learning Paradigms

Machine learning is broadly categorized into three paradigms:

  • Supervised Learning:
    Input Data: Requires labeled data (features and corresponding target labels).
    Feedback Loop: Direct feedback mechanism; predictions are compared to actual labels to calculate error.
    Target Applications: Classification (e.g., spam detection), Regression (e.g., house price prediction).
  • Unsupervised Learning:
    Input Data: Requires unlabeled data (only features, no target labels).
    Feedback Loop: No direct feedback; the model learns internal structures, patterns, or clusters autonomously.
    Target Applications: Clustering (e.g., customer segmentation), Dimensionality Reduction (e.g., PCA).
  • Reinforcement Learning:
    Input Data: No predefined dataset; an agent interacts with an environment represented as states.
    Feedback Loop: Delayed feedback in the form of rewards or penalties based on the sequence of actions taken.
    Target Applications: Robotics, game AI (e.g., AlphaGo), autonomous navigation.

title: 3. Define Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA). Describe how computing summary statistics and creating data visualizations aid in understanding raw datasets.
answer_html:
Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA)

Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA) is the initial investigative process performed on a dataset to discover patterns, spot anomalies, test hypotheses, and check assumptions with the help of summary statistics and graphical representations.

Role of Summary Statistics:

  • Metrics like mean, median, standard deviation, and percentiles provide a quantitative summary of feature distributions.
  • They help in quickly identifying central tendencies and the spread of data, pointing out potential outliers.

Role of Data Visualizations:

  • Histograms and Box plots: Reveal the skewness, spread, and exact outlier points in numerical data.
  • Scatter plots: Highlight correlations and relationships between two numerical variables.
  • Heatmaps: Visualize correlation matrices, helping to identify multicollinearity between features.
  • Visualizations make complex datasets interpretable and guide the subsequent feature engineering and modeling choices.

title: 4. Differentiate between Feature Engineering and Feature Selection. Explain the working principles of min-max scaling, standardization (z-score), and categorical label encoding.
answer_html:
Feature Engineering vs. Feature Selection

Feature Engineering involves creating new features or transforming existing ones to improve model performance (e.g., extracting day of the week from a date). Feature Selection involves choosing the most relevant subset of existing features to reduce dimensionality and noise without creating new ones.

Working Principles:

  • Min-Max Scaling: Transforms numerical features to a fixed range, typically [0, 1].
    Formula: $X_{scaled} = \frac{X - X_{min}}{X_{max} - X_{min}}$. Useful for algorithms that rely on distances (like KNN).
  • Standardization (Z-score): Transforms data to have a mean of 0 and standard deviation of 1.
    Formula: $Z = \frac{X - \mu}{\sigma}$. More robust to outliers than min-max scaling and preferred for gradient descent-based algorithms.
  • Categorical Label Encoding: Converts categorical string values into numerical integer representations (e.g., Red=0, Green=1, Blue=2). Necessary because ML algorithms require numerical input. However, it may introduce ordinal relationships implicitly; hence, One-Hot Encoding is sometimes preferred for nominal data.

title: 5. Discuss the importance of data collection and fetching strategies. Explain how uncleaned data issues like missing attributes or outliers degrade downstream ML model fitting.
answer_html:
Data Collection and Uncleaned Data Issues

Data collection is the foundation of any ML project. The quality, quantity, and representativeness of the fetched data directly govern the maximum possible performance of the predictive model. Strategies like automated API polling, web scraping, or database querying must ensure data integrity.

Impact of Uncleaned Data:

  • Missing Attributes: Algorithms may fail to process rows with NaN/Null values. If handled poorly (e.g., filling with zero instead of the mean), it distorts the feature distribution and misguides the learning process.
  • Outliers: Extreme outlier values severely skew models that minimize squared errors (like Linear Regression), as the squared penalty for outliers pulls the decision boundary or regression line away from the majority of the data.
  • Inconsistencies and Duplicates: Duplicate entries can cause overfitting to certain patterns, while inconsistencies (like mixed date formats) lead to feature misinterpretation and degraded model fitting.

title: 6. Derive the Ordinary Least Squares (OLS) error minimization framework for Simple Linear Regression and state its objective function.
answer_html:
Ordinary Least Squares (OLS)

Simple Linear Regression models the relationship between a dependent variable $y$ and an independent variable $x$ as: $\hat{y} = mx + c$, where $m$ is the slope and $c$ is the intercept.

Objective Function: The OLS method aims to minimize the Sum of Squared Residuals (SSR) between actual and predicted values. The cost function $J$ is:
$J(m, c) = \sum_{i=1}^{n} (y_i - \hat{y}_i)^2 = \sum_{i=1}^{n} (y_i - (mx_i + c))^2$

Derivation Framework:

  • To find the optimal $m$ and $c$, we take the partial derivatives of $J$ with respect to $m$ and $c$, and set them to zero.
  • $\frac{\partial J}{\partial c} = -2 \sum_{i=1}^{n} (y_i - mx_i - c) = 0 \implies \sum y_i = m\sum x_i + nc$
  • $\frac{\partial J}{\partial m} = -2 \sum_{i=1}^{n} x_i(y_i - mx_i - c) = 0 \implies \sum x_i y_i = m\sum x_i^2 + c\sum x_i$
  • Solving these two normal equations yields the optimal formulas for slope $m$ and intercept $c$, which represent the best-fit line minimizing the squared errors.

title: 7. Explain how the Gradient Descent optimization algorithm updates model weights iteratively. Contrast its performance against the analytical Normal Equation on high-dimensional datasets.
answer_html:
Gradient Descent vs Normal Equation

Gradient Descent (GD):

GD is an iterative optimization algorithm used to minimize a cost function $J(\theta)$. It updates model weights (parameters) by moving in the direction opposite to the gradient of the cost function with respect to the weights.

  • Update Rule: $\theta_j = \theta_j - \alpha \frac{\partial J(\theta)}{\partial \theta_j}$, where $\alpha$ is the learning rate.
  • It iteratively takes steps proportional to the negative gradient until it converges to a local or global minimum.

Contrast with Normal Equation:

  • The Normal Equation provides an analytical, closed-form solution to linear regression: $\theta = (X^T X)^{-1} X^T y$.
  • High-Dimensional Datasets: The Normal Equation requires computing the inverse of an $(n \times n)$ matrix ($X^T X$), which has a time complexity of $O(n^3)$. For large number of features (e.g., $n > 10,000$), matrix inversion becomes computationally prohibitive.
  • Gradient Descent scales much better with large numbers of features ($O(n^2)$ per iteration) and is highly preferred for high-dimensional datasets and models where analytical solutions do not exist.

title: 8. Describe Polynomial Regression and explain how higher-degree terms capture non-linear data patterns while maintaining a linear cost function structure.
answer_html:
Polynomial Regression

Polynomial Regression is an extension of linear regression that models the relationship between the independent variable $x$ and the dependent variable $y$ as an $n$-th degree polynomial.

Capturing Non-Linear Patterns:

  • Instead of a simple straight line ($y = \theta_0 + \theta_1x$), polynomial regression introduces higher-degree terms: $y = \theta_0 + \theta_1x + \theta_2x^2 + \dots + \theta_nx^n$.
  • These polynomial terms allow the regression curve to bend and flex, perfectly capturing non-linear trajectories and complex variance in the dataset.

Linear Cost Function Structure:

  • Despite fitting a non-linear curve to the data, Polynomial Regression is classified as a linear model.
  • This is because the model is linear with respect to the unknown parameters (weights $\theta_i$). If we define $x_1 = x$, $x_2 = x^2$, etc., the equation becomes $y = \theta_0 + \theta_1x_1 + \theta_2x_2 + \dots$, which is identical to multiple linear regression.
  • Therefore, the cost function (MSE) remains a convex quadratic bowl, and it can be solved using standard OLS or Gradient Descent without structural changes.

title: 9. Explain the concepts of Overfitting and Underfitting. Illustrate their relationship with model complexity, training vs. testing error rates, and the Bias-Variance Tradeoff.
answer_html:
Overfitting, Underfitting, and Bias-Variance Tradeoff

Underfitting (High Bias): Occurs when a model is too simple to capture the underlying data patterns. It performs poorly on both training and testing sets. This represents High Bias.

Overfitting (High Variance): Occurs when a model is excessively complex, learning the noise and fluctuations in the training data rather than the true signal. It performs exceptionally well on the training data but poorly on testing data. This represents High Variance.

Relationship with Model Complexity and Error Rates:

  • As model complexity increases, Training Error continuously decreases because the model fits the training points tighter.
  • Testing Error initially decreases as the model learns useful patterns, but eventually starts to increase when the model becomes too complex and begins overfitting.
  • Bias-Variance Tradeoff: The goal of ML is to find the "sweet spot" of model complexity that balances bias and variance, minimizing the total error (Testing Error). Too simple = high bias, too complex = high variance.

title: 10. Compare Ridge L2 and Lasso L1 Regularization. Explain why Lasso produces sparse solutions (zeroing weights) whereas Ridge shrinks coefficients without removing them.
answer_html:
Ridge (L2) vs Lasso (L1) Regularization

Regularization adds a penalty term to the cost function to prevent overfitting by penalizing large model weights.

Ridge Regularization (L2):

  • Cost Function: $J(\theta) = MSE + \lambda \sum_{i=1}^{n} \theta_i^2$
  • It adds the squared magnitude of coefficients as the penalty.
  • Shrinkage: Ridge shrinks all coefficients closer to zero but never exactly to zero. It handles multicollinearity well by distributing weights among correlated features.

Lasso Regularization (L1):

  • Cost Function: $J(\theta) = MSE + \lambda \sum_{i=1}^{n} |\theta_i|$
  • It adds the absolute value of coefficients as the penalty.
  • Sparse Solutions: The absolute value penalty creates a diamond-shaped constraint region. The elliptical contours of the MSE often intersect the diamond at its corners (where some coefficients are exactly zero).
  • Therefore, Lasso can completely eliminate less important features, performing automatic feature selection, resulting in sparse models.

title: 11. Detail the regression evaluation metrics: MAE, MSE, RMSE, and R2 Adjusted R2. Explain why RMSE and Adjusted R2 are preferred for model interpretation.
answer_html:
Regression Evaluation Metrics
  • Mean Absolute Error (MAE): $\frac{1}{n} \sum |y_i - \hat{y}_i|$. The average of absolute differences. Robust to outliers but gradient is undefined at zero.
  • Mean Squared Error (MSE): $\frac{1}{n} \sum (y_i - \hat{y}_i)^2$. Heavily penalizes large errors (outliers) due to squaring, making it useful for gradient descent. Units are squared.
  • Root Mean Squared Error (RMSE): $\sqrt{MSE}$. The square root brings the metric back to the original unit of the target variable.
  • R-Squared ($R^2$): Measures the proportion of variance in the dependent variable explained by the model. Range is 0 to 1. Higher is better.
  • Adjusted $R^2$: Modifies $R^2$ by penalizing the addition of non-useful predictive features.

Why RMSE and Adjusted $R^2$ are Preferred:

RMSE is highly preferred for interpretation because it is expressed in the same units as the target variable, making intuitive sense to stakeholders. Adjusted $R^2$ is preferred over standard $R^2$ in multiple regression because standard $R^2$ artificially increases whenever a new feature is added, even if it is irrelevant. Adjusted $R^2$ provides a more honest evaluation of the model\'s true explanatory power.

title: 12. Explain Logistic Regression for binary classification. Derive the Sigmoid activation function and state its mathematical properties.
answer_html:
Logistic Regression and Sigmoid Function

Logistic Regression is a supervised learning algorithm primarily used for binary classification. Unlike linear regression, which outputs continuous values, logistic regression squashes the output of a linear equation into a probability score between 0 and 1.

The Sigmoid Activation Function:

  • The linear component is $z = W^TX + b$. We pass $z$ through the Sigmoid function $\sigma(z)$ to get probabilities.
  • Formula: $\sigma(z) = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-z}}$

Mathematical Properties:

  • Range: The output of the sigmoid function is strictly bound between 0 and 1: $0 \le \sigma(z) \le 1$.
  • S-shaped Curve: The function maps large positive values close to 1, and large negative values close to 0.
  • Derivative: The derivative of the sigmoid function can be expressed in terms of itself, which makes gradient calculations computationally efficient: $\sigma\'(z) = \sigma(z)(1 - \sigma(z))$.
  • Decision Boundary: Typically, a threshold of 0.5 is used; if $\sigma(z) \ge 0.5$, class 1 is predicted; otherwise, class 0.

title: 13. Write the Log-Loss (Binary Cross-Entropy) cost function for Logistic Regression. Explain why standard MSE is non-convex and unsuitable for classification tasks.
answer_html:
Log-Loss (Binary Cross-Entropy)

The cost function for Logistic Regression is Log-Loss, also known as Binary Cross-Entropy.

Formula:

$J(\theta) = -\frac{1}{m} \sum_{i=1}^{m} \left[ y^{(i)} \log(h_\theta(x^{(i)})) + (1 - y^{(i)}) \log(1 - h_\theta(x^{(i)})) \right]$

Where $h_\theta(x)$ is the sigmoid predicted probability and $y$ is the actual binary label (0 or 1).

Why MSE is Unsuitable:

  • If we use standard Mean Squared Error (MSE) for Logistic Regression, the cost function becomes $J(\theta) = \frac{1}{2m} \sum (\sigma(W^TX) - y)^2$.
  • Because the sigmoid function $\sigma$ is non-linear, squaring it results in a non-convex cost function landscape with multiple local minima.
  • Gradient Descent is prone to getting stuck in these local minima, failing to find the global optimum.
  • Log-Loss, conversely, guarantees a convex cost function with a single global minimum, penalizing confident wrong predictions heavily using logarithms.

title: 14. Describe the complete prediction mechanics of the K-Nearest Neighbors (KNN) algorithm. Discuss how distance metric selection and varying choices of K impact boundary smoothness and error rates.
answer_html:
K-Nearest Neighbors (KNN) Algorithm

KNN is a non-parametric, instance-based, lazy learning algorithm used for both classification and regression.

Prediction Mechanics:

  1. Given a new data point, calculate the distance between it and all training points.
  2. Sort the calculated distances and identify the $K$ closest training data points (neighbors).
  3. For classification, apply majority voting among the $K$ neighbors. For regression, take the average of their values.

Impact of K and Distance Metrics:

  • Distance Metrics: Euclidean distance is standard for continuous data, while Manhattan distance is often better for high-dimensional or grid-like data. Minkowski distance acts as a generalization of both.
  • Small K (e.g., K=1): The decision boundary is highly irregular and captures local noise. This leads to low bias but high variance (overfitting).
  • Large K: The decision boundary becomes much smoother and generalized. However, if K is too large, it overlooks local patterns, leading to high bias and underfitting. A commonly used heuristic for K is $\sqrt{N}$.

title: 15. Explain how Decision Trees construct splits using Entropy, Gini Impurity, and Information Gain. State the mathematical formula for each metric.
answer_html:
Decision Tree Splitting Metrics

Decision Trees build classification models in the form of a tree structure by recursively splitting the dataset based on feature thresholds that maximize class separation purity.

  • Entropy: Measures the amount of impurity, disorder, or uncertainty in a node. A node with equal instances of all classes has maximum entropy (1.0 for binary), while a pure node has an entropy of 0.
    Formula: $E = -\sum_{i=1}^{c} p_i \log_2(p_i)$, where $p_i$ is the probability of class $i$.
  • Information Gain: The reduction in entropy after splitting a dataset on an attribute. The tree algorithm calculates Information Gain for every possible split and chooses the one with the highest gain.
    Formula: $IG(S, A) = Entropy(S) - \sum \left( \frac{|S_v|}{|S|} \right) Entropy(S_v)$
  • Gini Impurity: An alternative to entropy used by the CART algorithm. It measures the probability of misclassifying a randomly chosen element if it were randomly labeled according to the class distribution. It is computationally faster than entropy because it doesn\'t require logarithmic calculations.
    Formula: $Gini = 1 - \sum_{i=1}^{c} p_i^2$

title: 16. Explain the mathematical foundation of the Naive Bayes Classifier using Bayes\' Theorem. List all key assumptions made by the model regarding feature independence.
answer_html:
Naive Bayes Classifier

The Naive Bayes classifier is a probabilistic machine learning model based on Bayes\' Theorem, widely used for text classification tasks like spam filtering.

Mathematical Foundation:

  • Bayes\' Theorem states: $P(y|X) = \frac{P(X|y) \cdot P(y)}{P(X)}$
  • Where $P(y|X)$ is the posterior probability of class $y$ given features $X$.
  • $P(X|y)$ is the likelihood, and $P(y)$ is the prior probability of class $y$.

Key Assumptions (The "Naive" Aspect):

  • The core assumption is Conditional Independence of features. It assumes that the presence or absence of a particular feature (e.g., word A) is entirely independent of the presence of any other feature (e.g., word B), given the class variable.
  • Mathematically, the likelihood is decomposed as: $P(X|y) = P(x_1|y) \times P(x_2|y) \times \dots \times P(x_n|y)$.
  • Despite this assumption almost never holding perfectly true in real-world data (words in sentences are usually correlated), Naive Bayes often performs surprisingly well in practice.

title: 17. Describe Support Vector Machines (SVM). Explain the concepts of Hyperplanes, Support Vectors, Maximum Margin, and the difference between Hard Margin and Soft Margin (Hinge Loss).
answer_html:
Support Vector Machines (SVM)

SVM is a powerful algorithm that finds an optimal boundary between classes in an $N$-dimensional space.

  • Hyperplane: The decision boundary separating different classes. In 2D space, it\'s a line; in 3D, a flat plane.
  • Support Vectors: The specific data points lying closest to the hyperplane. They act as pillars; if they are moved or removed, the position of the dividing hyperplane alters. The algorithm only cares about these vectors.
  • Maximum Margin: SVM aims to find the hyperplane that maximizes the margin, which is the orthogonal distance between the hyperplane and the closest support vectors of each class. A wider margin implies better generalization.
  • Hard Margin vs. Soft Margin:
    - Hard Margin: Strictly separates classes without allowing any misclassification. Only works if data is perfectly linearly separable and is highly sensitive to outliers.
    - Soft Margin (Hinge Loss): Introduces a regularization parameter ($C$) and slack variables to allow a few misclassifications (errors). This yields a more robust, generalized boundary in the presence of noise or overlapping data.

title: 18. Explain the Kernel Trick in SVM. Describe how Linear, Polynomial, and Radial Basis Function (RBF) kernels enable the separation of non-linearly separable data.
answer_html:
SVM Kernel Trick

The Kernel Trick: Standard SVM only plots linear decision boundaries. When data is non-linearly separable, the "Kernel Trick" mathematically transforms the data into a higher-dimensional space where a linear hyperplane can separate the classes. It computes the dot products between data points in the expanded space efficiently, without explicitly materializing the higher-dimensional coordinates.

Types of Kernels:

  • Linear Kernel: Computes standard dot products. Used when data is linearly separable in its original feature space. Fastest to train.
  • Polynomial Kernel: Maps data into a polynomial feature space of degree $d$. Useful for data whose boundaries curve or form distinct shapes, commonly used in image processing.
  • Radial Basis Function (RBF) Kernel: The most popular kernel. It maps data into an infinite-dimensional space using exponential functions based on the distance between points (controlled by gamma $\gamma$). It can create highly localized, complex, island-like decision boundaries around clusters of data.

title: 19. Differentiate between Bagging and Boosting ensemble methods. Explain the voting/aggregation structure of Random Forests compared to sequential gradient boosting algorithms like XGBoost and AdaBoost.
answer_html:
Bagging vs. Boosting Ensemble Methods

Ensemble methods combine multiple weak machine learning models to create a single, highly accurate strong model.

Bagging (Bootstrap Aggregating) & Random Forest:

  • Concept: Trains multiple models independently and in parallel on random subsets of the training data (drawn with replacement).
  • Aggregation: Predictions are aggregated via majority voting (classification) or averaging (regression).
  • Random Forest: Uses bagging specifically on Decision Trees. It also uses random subsets of features at each split. It dramatically reduces variance (overfitting).

Boosting (XGBoost, AdaBoost):

  • Concept: Trains multiple models sequentially. Each new model specifically focuses on correcting the errors (misclassified instances or residuals) made by the previous models.
  • AdaBoost: Adjusts weights of data points, penalizing incorrect classifications more in the next round.
  • Gradient Boosting (XGBoost): Fits subsequent trees directly to the residual errors of the previous sequence.
  • Result: Primarily reduces bias (underfitting) and creates highly accurate models, though it is more prone to overfitting than Bagging if not tuned carefully.

title: 20. Construct a standard Confusion Matrix. Write the mathematical formulas for Accuracy, Precision, Recall, and F1-Score, explaining why F1-Score is critical for class-imbalanced data.
answer_html:
Confusion Matrix and Metrics

Confusion Matrix: A $2 \times 2$ table used to evaluate binary classification performance.

  • True Positive (TP): Predicted Positive, Actual Positive
  • True Negative (TN): Predicted Negative, Actual Negative
  • False Positive (FP - Type I Error): Predicted Positive, Actual Negative
  • False Negative (FN - Type II Error): Predicted Negative, Actual Positive

Evaluation Formulas:

  • Accuracy: $\frac{TP + TN}{TP + TN + FP + FN}$. The overall correct predictions.
  • Precision: $\frac{TP}{TP + FP}$. Out of all predicted positives, how many were actually positive?
  • Recall (Sensitivity): $\frac{TP}{TP + FN}$. Out of all actual positives, how many did the model find?
  • F1-Score: $2 \times \frac{Precision \times Recall}{Precision + Recall}$ (Harmonic Mean).

Importance of F1-Score for Imbalanced Data:
If a dataset has 99% Negative and 1% Positive instances, a model predicting "Negative" every time achieves 99% accuracy but fails its actual purpose. F1-Score completely ignores True Negatives, focusing strictly on the model\'s ability to correctly balance identifying the minority Positive class (Recall) without generating excessive false alarms (Precision).

title: A dataset contains the following observations of study hours (X) and examination marks (Y): X: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5. Y: 35, 40, 50, 55, 65. Find the simple linear regression equation y = b0 + b1x using the least-squares method. Predict the marks for a student who studies for 6 hours.
For the model y = b0 + b1x, the following data are given: n = 5, sum(x) = 20, sum(y) = 75, sum(x^2) = 90, sum(x*y) = 340. Calculate the values of b0 and b1, and write the final regression equation.

A fitted regression model is y = 12 + 4.5x, where x represents advertising expenditure in thousands of rupees and y represents sales in thousands of units. Calculate the predicted sales when advertising expenditure is 8,000 rupees. Also interpret the slope and intercept.
answer_html:
Step-by-step solution:

Model: y = 12 + 4.5x

x is in thousands, so for 8,000 rupees, x = 8.

Predicted sales y = 12 + 4.5(8) = 12 + 36 = 48 (i.e., 48,000 units).

Interpretation:

Slope (b1 = 4.5): For every 1,000 rupees increase in advertising expenditure, sales increase by 4,500 units.

Intercept (b0 = 12): If advertising expenditure is 0, the expected sales are 12,000 units.

title: Given the following observations: X: 2, 4, 6, 8, 10. Y: 4, 7, 8, 11, 14. Calculate x_bar, y_bar, the slope b1, and the intercept b0. Estimate Y when X = 12.

title: A logistic regression model produces the linear score z=2.5. Calculate the probability using the sigmoid function. If the classification threshold is 0.5, determine the predicted class.
answer_html:
Step-by-step solution:

z = 2.5

Sigmoid function: P = 1 / (1 + e^(-z))

P = 1 / (1 + e^(-2.5)) ≈ 1 / (1 + 0.082) ≈ 1 / 1.082 ≈ 0.924

Since P = 0.924 > 0.5 (threshold), the predicted class is 1.

title: For a sample, the logistic regression model produces z=-1.8. Calculate the sigmoid probability and determine whether the sample belongs to class 0 or class 1 using a threshold of 0.5.
answer_html:
Step-by-step solution:

z = -1.8

Sigmoid function: P = 1 / (1 + e^(-z))

P = 1 / (1 + e^(1.8)) ≈ 1 / (1 + 6.0496) ≈ 1 / 7.0496 ≈ 0.1418

Since P = 0.1418 < 0.5 (threshold), the sample belongs to Class 0.

title: Consider the logistic regression model z = -3 + 0.8x1 + 1.2x2. For a data point x1=2, x2=1: Calculate z, calculate the sigmoid probability, predict the class using threshold 0.5.
A binary classification model predicts the following probabilities for four observations: Actual y: 1, 1, 0, 0. Predicted p: 0.9, 0.7, 0.2, 0.4. Calculate the binary cross-entropy/log-loss.

KNN - Consider the following training data: Point A: (1,1, C=0), B: (2,2, C=0), C: (3,2, C=1), D: (5,4, C=1), E: (6,5, C=1). For query Q=(4,3), calculate distance from every point and classify using K=3.
For points P = (2,5), Q = (7,9), calculate: Euclidean distance, Manhattan distance, Squared Euclidean distance. Explain which metric gives the smallest numerical value.
answer_html:
Step-by-step solution:

  • Euclidean distance: √((7-2)² + (9-5)²) = √(5² + 4²) = √(25 + 16) = √41 ≈ 6.40
  • Manhattan distance: |7-2| + |9-5| = 5 + 4 = 9
  • Squared Euclidean: (7-2)² + (9-5)² = 25 + 16 = 41

Euclidean distance gives the smallest numerical value (6.40) because it measures the direct straight-line distance, whereas Manhattan measures along grid lines and Squared Euclidean squares the Euclidean distance (which is > 1 here).

title: Decision tree: A dataset contains 10 samples: 6 samples belong to Class A, 4 samples belong to Class B. Calculate the entropy.
Information gain: Parent 10 (6+, 4-). Left child: 5 (4+, 1-). Right child: 5 (2+, 3-). Calculate: Entropy of parent, left child, right child, Weighted entropy, Information Gain.
answer_html:
Step-by-step solution:

Parent node: 6+, 4-. Total = 10.
Entropy(Parent) = -0.6*log2(0.6) - 0.4*log2(0.4) ≈ 0.971

Left child: 4+, 1-. Total = 5.
Entropy(Left) = -0.8*log2(0.8) - 0.2*log2(0.2) ≈ 0.2575 + 0.4644 = 0.722

Right child: 2+, 3-. Total = 5.
Entropy(Right) = -0.4*log2(0.4) - 0.6*log2(0.6) ≈ 0.971

Weighted entropy:
(5/10)*0.722 + (5/10)*0.971 = 0.361 + 0.4855 = 0.8465

Information Gain:
Entropy(Parent) - Weighted entropy = 0.971 - 0.8465 = 0.1245

title: A parent node has 20 observations: 12 Class A, 8 Class B. A proposed split produces: Left: 8 A, 2 B. Right: 4 A, 6 B. Calculate the weighted Gini impurity of the split.
answer_html:

Left node: 8 A, 2 B (Total 10)
Gini(Left) = 1 - (8/10)² - (2/10)² = 1 - 0.64 - 0.04 = 0.32

Right node: 4 A, 6 B (Total 10)
Gini(Right) = 1 - (4/10)² - (6/10)² = 1 - 0.16 - 0.36 = 0.48

Weighted Gini:
Weight_Left = 10/20 = 0.5, Weight_Right = 10/20 = 0.5
Weighted Gini = (0.5 * 0.32) + (0.5 * 0.48) = 0.16 + 0.24 = 0.40

title: Suppose a spam classifier has: P(Spam) = 0.4, P(NotSpam) = 0.6. For an email containing words W1 and W2: P(W1|Spam)=0.7, P(W2|Spam)=0.8, P(W1|NotSpam)=0.2, P(W2|NotSpam)=0.3. Using Naive Bayes, determine whether the email is Spam or Not Spam.
answer_html:
Step-by-step solution:

We calculate the unnormalized posterior probabilities:

For Spam:
Score(Spam) = P(Spam) * P(W1|Spam) * P(W2|Spam)
Score(Spam) = 0.4 * 0.7 * 0.8 = 0.28 * 0.8 = 0.224

For Not Spam:
Score(NotSpam) = P(NotSpam) * P(W1|NotSpam) * P(W2|NotSpam)
Score(NotSpam) = 0.6 * 0.2 * 0.3 = 0.12 * 0.3 = 0.036

Since 0.224 > 0.036, the email is classified as Spam.

title: Support vector machine: An SVM hyperplane is 2x1 + 3x2 - 6 = 0. Determine the class of the following points using f(x) = w^Tx + b and the rule f(x)>0 -> Class +1, f(x)<0 -> Class -1. Points: P1 = (1,1), P2 = (2,2), P3 = (0,1).
Three regression trees predict the house price as: Tree 1 = 50 lakh, Tree 2 = 55 lakh, Tree 3 = 52 lakh. Calculate the Random Forest prediction using averaging.
answer_html:
Step-by-step solution:

Random forest regression uses the average of the predictions of the individual trees.

Prediction = (50 + 55 + 52) / 3 = 157 / 3 = 52.33 lakh

title: Three regression trees have predictions and weights: T1: Pred=100, W=0.2; T2: Pred=120, W=0.5; T3: Pred=110, W=0.3. Calculate the weighted ensemble prediction.
answer_html:
Step-by-step solution:

Weighted Prediction = (Pred1 * W1) + (Pred2 * W2) + (Pred3 * W3)

Since sum of weights = 0.2 + 0.5 + 0.3 = 1.0, we just calculate the dot product.

Prediction = (100 * 0.2) + (120 * 0.5) + (110 * 0.3)

Prediction = 20 + 60 + 33 = 113

title: Multiple boosting rounds: Initial prediction: F0(x) = 20. Three weak learners produce corrections: h1(x)=10, h2(x)=6, h3(x)=4 with learning rate = 0.2. Calculate F3(x).
A weak classifier correctly classifies 80 out of 100 training samples. Calculate its error rate and classifier weight.
answer_html:
Step-by-step solution:

Total samples = 100, Correct = 80, Incorrect = 20.

Error rate (ε): 20 / 100 = 0.2

Classifier weight (α): calculated using the Adaboost formula: α = 0.5 * ln((1 - ε) / ε)

α = 0.5 * ln((1 - 0.2) / 0.2) = 0.5 * ln(0.8 / 0.2) = 0.5 * ln(4)

α = 0.5 * 1.386 = 0.693

title: A binary classifier produces: TP=80, TN=70, FP=10, FN=20. Calculate: Accuracy, Precision, Recall, F1-score.

A binary classification model gives the following probabilities: Sample 1(A=1, P=0.9), 2(0, 0.2), 3(1, 0.7), 4(0, 0.6), 5(1, 0.8), 6(0, 0.1), 7(1, 0.4), 8(0, 0.3). Using threshold 0.5: Determine predicted classes, Construct the confusion matrix, Calculate accuracy, precision, recall, F1-score, and log-loss.
answer_html:
Step-by-step solution:

Predictions (Threshold = 0.5):

  • S1: Act=1, Prob=0.9 -> Pred=1 (TP)
  • S2: Act=0, Prob=0.2 -> Pred=0 (TN)
  • S3: Act=1, Prob=0.7 -> Pred=1 (TP)
  • S4: Act=0, Prob=0.6 -> Pred=1 (FP)
  • S5: Act=1, Prob=0.8 -> Pred=1 (TP)
  • S6: Act=0, Prob=0.1 -> Pred=0 (TN)
  • S7: Act=1, Prob=0.4 -> Pred=0 (FN)
  • S8: Act=0, Prob=0.3 -> Pred=0 (TN)

Confusion Matrix:

Predicted 1Predicted 0
Actual 1TP = 3FN = 1
Actual 0FP = 1TN = 3

Metrics:

  • Accuracy = (3+3)/8 = 6/8 = 0.75
  • Precision = 3/(3+1) = 3/4 = 0.75
  • Recall = 3/(3+1) = 3/4 = 0.75
  • F1-score = 2(0.75*0.75)/(0.75+0.75) = 0.75

Log-loss: -1/8 * Σ [y*ln(p) + (1-y)*ln(1-p)]

Sum = ln(0.9) + ln(0.8) + ln(0.7) + ln(0.4) + ln(0.8) + ln(0.9) + ln(0.4) + ln(0.7)
(S1=1:ln(0.9), S2=0:ln(0.8), S3=1:ln(0.7), S4=0:ln(0.4), S5=1:ln(0.8), S6=0:ln(0.9), S7=1:ln(0.4), S8=0:ln(0.7))

Sum ≈ -0.105 - 0.223 - 0.357 - 0.916 - 0.223 - 0.105 - 0.916 - 0.357 = -3.202

Log-loss = -1/8 * (-3.202) = 0.400

title: A decision tree predicts disease status for 100 patients: 35 true positives, 45 true negatives, 10 false positives, 10 false negatives. Calculate: Entropy of the complete dataset, Gini impurity, Accuracy, Precision, Recall, F1-score.
Three models provide predictions for a regression problem. Calculate the MAE and MSE for each model and determine which model performs best.
answer_html:
Step-by-step solution:

Actuals: 100, 200, 150, 300

Random Forest (RF): Preds = 95, 210, 145, 290

  • Errors: -5, 10, -5, -10
  • Abs Errors: 5, 10, 5, 10 -> MAE = 30/4 = 7.5
  • Sq Errors: 25, 100, 25, 100 -> MSE = 250/4 = 62.5

Gradient Boosting (GB): Preds = 98, 205, 148, 295

  • Errors: -2, 5, -2, -5
  • Abs Errors: 2, 5, 2, 5 -> MAE = 14/4 = 3.5
  • Sq Errors: 4, 25, 4, 25 -> MSE = 58/4 = 14.5

XGBoost (XGB): Preds = 99, 202, 152, 298

  • Errors: -1, 2, 2, -2
  • Abs Errors: 1, 2, 2, 2 -> MAE = 7/4 = 1.75
  • Sq Errors: 1, 4, 4, 4 -> MSE = 13/4 = 3.25

Conclusion: XGBoost performs best because it has the lowest MAE and MSE.
